*A companion to the syllabus. The readings are a bank, not a week-by-week assignment: they are grouped by theme, and I will name the specific ones for each session about a week ahead. Suggestions are welcome. The second half is the practical guide to R and Quarto — treat "Setting up" as your week-one checklist and the rest as reference.*

### Who pays for the infrastructure --- a live case, autumn 2026

*The Center for Open Science announced in August 2026 that it is retiring the OSF Projects workflow: no new projects after 16 November 2026, all projects read-only from 19 February 2027. Registrations and preprints continue. This is our week 13 case study, and it is worth more than a footnote --- the field built a decade of open practice on one nonprofit's free tier.*

Center for Open Science. (2026). *OSF changes.* --- <https://www.cos.io/osf-changes>, with the transition details at <https://help.osf.io/article/759-details-of-osf-projects-transition>

Nature news. (2026). Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns. *Nature.* --- <https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02598-y>

Simonsohn, U., Nelson, L. D., & Simmons, J. P. (2026). \[137\] OSF will stop accepting your research files, you can use ResearchBox instead. *Data Colada.* --- <https://datacolada.org/137>

*Questions worth holding onto: if "open" depends on a platform that can withdraw a service, what exactly was open? Does a DOI that resolves to a read-only archive satisfy a data-availability statement? And who should be paying --- funders, libraries, journals, or nobody?*

*On the limits of transparency:* "When all findings are made available, (a) it is harder to discriminate the true findings from the false findings, and (b) there will be more false findings." --- a claim worth arguing about in week 13.

# R and Quarto

*You will do all analysis in R and write in Quarto. Prior R experience helps but is not assumed.*

::: panel-tabset
## Setting up

Install, in this order:

1.  **R** (latest release) --- <https://cran.r-project.org>
2.  **RStudio Desktop** --- <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>. Quarto is with recent RStudio; you can also install Quarto separately from <https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/>.
3.  **Git**, and a GitHub account --- <https://happygitwithr.com> is the definitive guide to getting Git, GitHub, and RStudio talking to one another. Budget an evening; it is a highest-return hour of setup in this course.
4.  A **Zenodo account** --- <https://zenodo.org> --- signed in with GitHub, with the GitHub--Zenodo integration switched on for your project repository (<https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content>). Every GitHub release then becomes an archived, DOI-bearing snapshot automatically. Add a `CITATION.cff` file to the repository so the citation metadata is machine-readable.
5.  An **OSF account** --- <https://osf.io> --- for your preregistration. Note that OSF Projects are being retired (no new projects after 16 November 2026; read-only from 19 February 2027); **Registries and Preprints continue unaffected**, and that is all we will use OSF for. You will still read plenty of other people's OSF project archives, which remain viewable and downloadable.
6.  **Zotero** plus the **Better BibTeX** extension --- <https://www.zotero.org>, <https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/>. Export your library to a `.bib` file that Quarto cites from directly.

Verify your setup by rendering a Quarto document to HTML and to Word in week one. If that works, everything else is detail.

## Project hygiene

Three habits, adopted now, will save your project later.

- **One RStudio Project per study**, with a folder structure you decide once: `data/raw/` (never written to), `data/processed/`, `R/`, `analysis/`, `output/`. Use the `here` package for paths, never `setwd()`.
- **Record your dependencies.** `renv` snapshots the exact package versions your analysis used, so that the project still runs next year. `renv::init()` at the start, `renv::snapshot()` whenever you add a package.
- **Commit often, with messages that mean something.** Version control is what lets your co-authors work on your project without sending files back and forth, and it is the evidence trail your contribution grade reads.

## Core stack

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "renv", "janitor", "quarto"))

`tidyverse` for data manipulation and graphics (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `ggplot2`, `readr`, `stringr`, `purrr`), `janitor` for cleaning imported spreadsheets, `here` for paths.

## Packages

Install by track; nobody needs all of these.

### Forensic and evidential-value tools (Track A)

| Package | What it does |
|:---|:---|
| `statcheck` | Extracts reported NHST results from papers and recomputes p-values; the workhorse of reporting-consistency audits |
| `zcurve` | Z-curve 2.0 --- estimates expected replicability and observed/expected discovery rates from a set of test statistics |
| `dmetar` | Companion to *Doing Meta-Analysis in R*; includes p-curve, power analysis, and bias diagnostics |
| `puniform` | p-uniform and p-uniform\* --- effect-size estimation corrected for publication bias |
| `metafor` | The comprehensive meta-analysis package; also the base most bias-correction methods build on |
| `PublicationBias` | Sensitivity analysis for publication bias (Mathur & VanderWeele) |
| `RoBMA` | Robust Bayesian meta-analysis --- model-averaged estimates across publication-bias models |
| `metasens` | Further sensitivity methods, including limit meta-analysis and Copas selection |
| `scrutiny` | GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT --- consistency tests for reported summary statistics |
| `rsprite2` | SPRITE --- reconstructs plausible raw data from reported means and SDs |
| `pwr`, `Superpower` | Power analysis for the standard tests and for factorial designs |
| `effectsize`, `esc`, `effsize` | Effect-size computation and conversion between metrics |
| `TOSTER` | Equivalence testing and the "small telescopes" family of replication evaluations |

### Corpus building and screening (both tracks)

| Package | What it does |
|:---|:---|
| `openalexR` | Queries OpenAlex --- the most useful free bibliographic API for building a sampling frame |
| `rcrossref` | Crossref metadata, including DOIs, licences, and funder information |
| `roadoi` | Resolves open-access status and full-text locations via Unpaywall |
| `revtools`, `synthesisr`, `litsearchr` | Systematic-review workflow: import, deduplicate, screen, and design search strings |
| `pdftools` | Extracts text from PDFs; the entry point for automated coding of article corpora |
| `osfr` | Talks to the OSF API from R --- still the fastest way to pull down the many existing OSF archives your corpus will point at |
| `zen4R` | Zenodo API from R --- deposit, version, and retrieve archives programmatically |

### Reporting and manuscripts

| Package | What it does |
|:---|:---|
| `papaja` | APA 7 manuscripts from R Markdown, with automatic statistical reporting |
| `apaquarto` | The Quarto equivalent --- an extension, installed per-project, not a package |
| `gt`, `flextable`, `tinytable` | Publication-quality tables; `flextable` is the reliable route into Word |
| `targets` | Pipeline management for analyses too large to re-run by hand |

## Quarto

Quarto is the writing environment for this course: prose, code, results, figures, tables, and citations in one file that renders to Word, PDF, or HTML. The point is not elegance. The point is that the number in your manuscript is computed by the code beside it, so it cannot drift out of date, and a reader with your files can reproduce it exactly.

A minimal document:

```` markdown
---
title: "Evidential value in the third-person effect literature"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: custom-reference.docx
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

## Method

We identified `r nrow(studies)` eligible studies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pcurve
#| fig-cap: "P-curve for the focal test statistics."
plot_pcurve(studies)
```

As @fig-pcurve shows, ...
````

Things worth learning early, roughly in order of return:

- **Chunk options** (`#| label:`, `#| echo:`, `#| fig-cap:`) --- labelled chunks are what make cross-references work.
- **Inline code** --- `` `r nrow(studies)` `` writes a computed number into your prose. Use it for every number in the manuscript.
- **Cross-references** --- `@fig-pcurve`, `@tbl-coding`, `@sec-method`. Numbering takes care of itself.
- **Citations** --- `[@simmons2011]` from your `.bib` file, with a CSL style file for APA 7 (<https://www.zotero.org/styles>).
- **Rendering to Word** with a `reference-doc` --- the fastest route to a document a co-author can comment on in track changes. For a full APA 7 manuscript, use `apaquarto` (<https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/>).
- **Freezing and caching** (`execute: freeze: auto`) once your analysis takes more than a few seconds to run.

## Where to learn

**R**

- R/Markdown guide: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qk8uIXyCPVLUTpXhzW069A0qbyZgaFfw9KaNV4ZI8w4/edit?tab=t.0>
- Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund, *R for Data Science* (2nd ed.) --- <https://r4ds.hadley.nz>. The standard introduction; free.
- *Happy Git and GitHub for the useR* --- <https://happygitwithr.com>
- Lakens, *Improving Your Statistical Inferences* --- <https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/>. The best free resource connecting statistical reasoning to open-science practice, with R throughout. Much of our week 6--7 material is here.
- Harrer et al., *Doing Meta-Analysis in R* --- <https://bookdown.org/MathiasHarrer/Doing_Meta_Analysis_in_R/>
- Matthew B. Jané, effect-size resources --- <https://matthewbjane.quarto.pub>

**Quarto**

- Official documentation --- <https://quarto.org/docs/guide/>. Unusually good; start with the Authoring and Output Formats sections.
- Introduction to Quarto for Research projects — <https://pythonhealthdatascience.github.io/quarto-tutorial/>
- FAIR & Reproducible Teaching with Quarto & Git — <https://lennartwittkuhn.com/fair-teaching-course/schedule.html>
- Quarto for Scientists --- <https://qmd4sci.njtierney.com/>
- `apaquarto` documentation --- <https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/>

**Reproducible workflow**

- Wilson, Bryan, Cranston, Kitzes, Nederbragt & Teal (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. *PLOS Computational Biology*, 13(6), e1005510.
- The Turing Way --- <https://the-turing-way.netlify.app>
- FORRT resources --- <https://forrt.org/clusters/>

**When you are stuck**

Post the problem to the seminar channel with a *reproducible example* --- the smallest piece of code that fails, plus the data it needs. Constructing one solves the problem outright surprisingly often. The `reprex` package does the packaging for you.
